Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verses 1–2:

(p-107) Surat ʿAbasa is Meccan, and its verses number forty-two.

﴿He frowned and turned away﴾ ﴿because the blind man came to him.﴾ It is narrated that Ibn Umm Maktum, whose name was ʿAbd Allah ibn Shurayh ibn Malik ibn Abi Rabiʿa al-Fihri, and Umm Maktum being the name of his father's mother, "came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) while with him were the chieftains of Quraysh: ʿUtba and Shayba, the two sons of Rabiʿa, Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, Umayya ibn Khalaf, and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, whom he was calling to Islam, hoping that by their Islam others would embrace it. He said to him: 'O Messenger of God, teach me and instruct me in what God has taught you,' and he repeated that, not knowing that he (ﷺ) was occupied with the people. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) disliked cutting off his speech, so he frowned and turned away from him; then this was revealed." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) would honor him, and when he saw him he would say: "Welcome to one whom my Lord rebuked me about," and he would say to him: "Do you have any need?" He appointed him as his deputy over Medina twice.

It is read ("ʿabbasa") with the doubled letter for emphasis (al-mubalagha). "Because the blind man came to him" is the cause (ʿilla) of "turned away." Or it is read ("ʿabasa") according to the difference of the two opinions, meaning: because the blind man came to him. Mentioning the attribute of his blindness is either to prepare an excuse for his action of cutting off his speech (ﷺ) with the people, and to indicate that he deserves gentleness and compassion, or to intensify the rebuke, as if it were said: he turned away because he is blind, just as the shift (iltifat) in the words of the Exalted...

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verses 1–2:

(p-107) Surat ʿAbasa is Meccan, and its verses number forty-two.

﴿He frowned and turned away﴾ ﴿because the blind man came to him.﴾ It is narrated that Ibn Umm Maktum, whose name was ʿAbd Allah ibn Shurayh ibn Malik ibn Abi Rabiʿa al-Fihri, and Umm Maktum being the name of his father's mother, "came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) while with him were the chieftains of Quraysh: ʿUtba and Shayba, the two sons of Rabiʿa, Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, Umayya ibn Khalaf, and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, whom he was calling to Islam, hoping that by their Islam others would embrace it. He said to him: 'O Messenger of God, teach me and instruct me in what God has taught you,' and he repeated that, not knowing that he (ﷺ) was occupied with the people. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) disliked cutting off his speech, so he frowned and turned away from him; then this was revealed." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) would honor him, and when he saw him he would say: "Welcome to one whom my Lord rebuked me about," and he would say to him: "Do you have any need?" He appointed him as his deputy over Medina twice.

It is read ("ʿabbasa") with the doubled letter for emphasis (al-mubalagha). "Because the blind man came to him" is the cause (ʿilla) of "turned away." Or it is read ("ʿabasa") according to the difference of the two opinions, meaning: because the blind man came to him. Mentioning the attribute of his blindness is either to prepare an excuse for his action of cutting off his speech (ﷺ) with the people, and to indicate that he deserves gentleness and compassion, or to intensify the rebuke, as if it were said: he turned away because he is blind, just as the shift (iltifat) in the words of the Exalted...

"And what could make you know" — as to that, direct address is more effective in intensifying the reproach. That is: and what makes you aware of his condition, such that you turn away from him? His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps he would purify himself﴾ is a resumed (isti'nafi) clause coming to explain what the preceding statement hints at. For it, along with its indicating that he has a matter incompatible with turning away from him, a matter beyond the knowledge and perception of others, signals that God, exalted is He, is the One who makes him aware of that. That is: perhaps he would purify himself through what he would take from you of the burdens of sins, entirely. The word "perhaps" (la'alla), even with the certainty of purification, comes in accordance with the manner of majesty (kibriya'), or, on the basis of the meaning of hope (tarajji) with respect to him, peace and blessings be upon him, to alert that turning away from him when he is hoped to purify himself is impermissible, so how much more so when purification is certain, as in your saying: "Perhaps you will regret what you did?" And in it is an indication that those among the disbelievers whom he addresses for their purification are not hoped, at all, to purify themselves or to be mindful.

(p-108) And His saying, Most High: ﴿Or he would be reminded, and the reminder would benefit him﴾.

﴿Or he would be reminded﴾ is conjoined (ʿatf) to "yazzakkā" (he might purify himself), and so falls under the same ruling of hope (taraji). His saying, Most High:

"fa-tanfaʿahu al-dhikrā" (and the reminder would benefit him)

is in the accusative (naṣb) as the answer (jawab) to "laʿalla" (perhaps). It has also been read in the nominative (rafʿ), as a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "yadhdhakkaru" (he would be reminded), meaning: "or he would remember, and your admonition would benefit him, if he has not reached the degree of complete purification." It has also been said that the pronoun in "laʿallahu" refers to the disbeliever, so the meaning is: you hoped that he would purify himself, or be reminded, and the reminder would bring him closer to accepting the truth; and for this reason you turned away from the blind man. And what would make you know that this is something whose occurrence is hoped for?

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 80, verse 5:

﴿As for he who considers himself self-sufficient﴾, i.e., who is independent of faith and of what you possess of the knowledge and insights that the Qur'an contains.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verse 6:**

﴿Yet you give attention to him﴾, that is: you direct yourself toward him, showing eagerness to face him, and taking care to guide him and to set him on the right path. In this there is further rebuke to him, upon him be blessings and peace (ﷺ), against keeping company with them, for turning toward the one who turns his back (al-mudabbir) is not among the habits of the great. It is also read as (تَصَّدّى) with the tā' assimilated into the ṣād, and it is read as (تُصْدى) with a ḍammah on the tā', meaning: he is presented to you, and its meaning is that a call summons you to attend to him, out of a desire and an intense eagerness for his Islam.

"And what is it to you if he does not purify himself?" There is no fault upon you in that he does not purify himself through Islam, until you concern yourself with his affair and turn away from the one who has embraced Islam. The clause is a circumstantial (hal) clause referring to the pronoun in "taṣaddā" (you attend to him). It has also been said that "mā" is interrogative, used for denial, meaning: "What is upon you regarding his not purifying himself?" Its ultimate sense is also negation.
﴿But as for he who comes to you eagerly﴾. That is: while he is coming hastily, seeking what you have of the rulings of right guidance (rushd) and the qualities of goodness.

﴿وَهُوَ يَخْشى﴾ (and he fears). That is, Allah the Exalted. It has also been said: he fears the harm of the disbelievers in coming to you. And it has been said: he fears stumbling, since he had no guide with him. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the subject of "yas'a" (he hastens), just as it is also a circumstantial clause referring to the subject of "jaa'aka" (came to you).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verse 10:

﴿Then you (Muhammad) are distracted from him.﴾ Tatashaghalu (you busy yourself). It is said: lahiya 'anhu, and iltahā, and talahhā (he was diverted from it / he occupied himself away from it). It is also read: (tatalahhā) and talahhā, meaning: the concern for the notables (al-sanādīd) distracts you. The placing of his pronoun, upon him be the prayer and peace, before the two verbs is an alert that the basis of the denunciation is his particular status, upon him be the prayer and peace; that is, someone like you in particular should not turn toward the one who is self-sufficient and be distracted from the poor seeker of goodness. The placing of "lahu" and "'anhu" is for an allusion to his concern, upon him be the prayer and peace, with what both of them contain.

It is narrated that he, upon him be the prayer and peace, said: ﴿He never frowned again at a poor man, nor did he ever turn toward a rich man.﴾

﴿Nay!﴾ (p-109) It is a rebuke to him, peace and blessings be upon him, for what he was reproached for: giving his attention to the one who considered himself free of what he was called to, namely faith and obedience and what entails them from the Noble Qur'an. He was overly concerned with his affair and zealously eager for his acceptance of Islam, and because of this he turned away from guiding one who sought his guidance. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Indeed, it is a reminder﴾, that is, an admonition by which one must be admonished and act according to what it requires, is a justification (ta'lil) for the rebuke concerning what was mentioned. It demonstrates the exalted rank of the Mighty Qur'an, which the one he was attending to had dispensed with, and it establishes that its nature is to be an admonition truly worthy of being heeded. Thus whoever desires it is admonished by it, as expressed by His saying, may He be exalted:

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 80, verse 12:

﴿Whoever wills, remembers it﴾, meaning: he preserves it and takes admonition from it. As for one who turns away from it, like the one who considers himself self-sufficient (al-mustaghni), there is no need to concern oneself with his affair. The two pronouns (الضَّمِيرانِ) refer to the Qur'an, and the feminine form is used, the first because its predicate (خَبَرُهُ) is feminine. It has been said that the first refers to the surah, or to the preceding verses, and the second to the reminder (التَّذْكِرَةِ) and the admonition (التَّذْكِيرِ), since they carry the sense of remembrance (الذِّكْرِ) and exhortation (الوَعْظِ). But this is not the correct view. The surah and the verses, although they possess the noble attributes that will come later, are not among the things cast upon the one who has turned away from them and who deserved, because of that, what will follow of supplication against him and wonder at his excessive disbelief, since their revelation came after the incident. As for one who permitted their (the pronouns') return to the aforementioned rebuke, he has erred, committed a breach of etiquette, and blundered in a way that causes astonishment. So reflect, and be upon the manifest truth. And His, the Exalted's, statement:

In suhuf (scrolls/pages) — this is connected to a hidden verb and is an attribute of "a reminder." What lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD), brought in to encourage it and urge its memorization; that is, it exists in scrolls copied from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh). Or it is a second predicate of "inna" (indeed): ﴿honored﴾ with Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verse 14:

﴿Exalted﴾ i.e., in the seventh heaven, or exalted in rank and mention.

﴿Purified﴾ free from being touched by the hands of the devils.

﴿بِأيْدِي سَفَرَةٍ﴾ (*bi-aydi safaratin*, "in the hands of scribes"), that is, scribes from among the angels who copy the books from the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh*), understood as the plural of *safir* (سافِرٍ), from *al-sifr* (السِّفْر), meaning books. It was also said: "in the hands of messenger angels who carry the revelation between Him, exalted is He, and the prophets," understood as the plural of *safir* (سَفِيرٍ), from *al-sifara* (السِّفارَة), meaning intermediary. However, taking them to be the prophets, peace be upon them, is far-fetched, for their function is to receive revelation, not to copy books from it, and to guide the community through commands and prohibitions and to teach the laws and rulings, not merely to act as intermediaries to them. Likewise, taking them to be the reciters (*al-qurra'*, القُرّاءِ) because they recite the books (*al-asfar*, الأسْفارَ), or to be the Companions of the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace. They have said that this term is specific to the angels and is hardly used of anyone else, although its use for others is permissible according to the lexical usage. The preposition *bi* (الباءُ) is connected to "*mutahhara*" (مُطَهَّرَةٍ, "purified"). Al-Qaffal said: since none touches it except the purified angels, the purity was ascribed to it because of the purity of those who touch it. Al-Qurtubi said: the intended meaning of what is in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿لا يَمَسُّهُ إلا المُطَهَّرُونَ﴾ ("None touches it except the purified"), is these noble, obedient scribes.

(p-110) ﴿Noble﴾ before Allah, Mighty and Majestic; or ones who show compassion to the believers, speaking with them and asking forgiveness for them.

﴿Pious﴾ (abrar), i.e., God-fearing. It has also been said: obedient to Allah, Exalted is He, from their saying, "So-and-so is dutiful to his Creator" (yabarru khaliqahu), meaning he obeys Him. It has also been said: truthful, from one who fulfills his oath (bara fi yaminihi).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verse 17:

﴿Woe to man!﴾ It is a supplication against him with the most grievous of curses. His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿How ungrateful he is!﴾ is an expression of wonder at his excessive disbelief (kufran) and a statement of his deserving to be cursed. What is meant by "man" is either the one who has become independent of the Noble Qur'an, whose sublime attributes necessitate turning to it and believing in it, or the species, considered in terms of its inclusion of him and his like among its individuals, not in terms of all of its individuals. In this, together with the brevity of its text (matn) and the closeness of its two extremes (qutrayh), there is an announcement of great wrath and extreme blame beyond which there is no further limit. His, may He be exalted, saying:

"From what thing did He create him?" This begins the explanation of his excessive ingratitude (kufran), by detailing the various kinds of blessings that He bestowed upon him from the beginning of his natural disposition (fitrah) to the end of his life, blessings which call for gratitude and obedience, while he neglects that obligation; and [it begins] with a question about the origin of his creation, followed by its explanation in the words of the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verse 19:

﴿From a drop of sperm He created him﴾ is a belittling of him: that is, from a worthless, contemptible thing He created him, from a foul-smelling drop of sperm He created him. ﴿Then He proportioned him﴾ meaning He prepared him for what is fitting and suitable for him of limbs and forms, or [it means] He proportioned him in stages until his creation was completed. And the words of the Exalted:

Then He made the way easy for him (﴿ثُمَّ السَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُ﴾). The word "the way" (al-sabil) is in the accusative, governed by a implied verb that is explained by the apparent one, meaning: then He facilitated his exit from the belly, by opening the mouth of the womb and inspiring him to turn (into the proper position for birth); or, He made the way of good and evil easy for him and empowered him to traverse it. The definiteness of "the way" by means of the definite article, rather than by an annexed construction, indicates its generality.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verse 21:

﴿Then He caused him to die and made him to be buried.﴾ That is: He made him one who has a grave in which he is concealed, as an honour to him, and did not leave him cast out upon the face of the earth, a dry and barren place, for beasts of prey and birds, like the rest of the animals. It is said: "qabara al-mayyit" (he buried the dead) when he interred him, and "aqbarahu" (he caused him to be buried) when he commanded that he be buried or was enabled to do so. Counting death among the blessings is because it is, in a general sense, a means of reaching eternal life and everlasting bliss.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verse 22:

﴿Then, when He wills, He will raise him up again.﴾ That is: when He wills, He raises him up (anshara-hu, "raised him to life again"). This is in accordance with the established practice of omitting the object of the verb of willing (al-mashi'ah), and in linking the resurrection (al-insharr) to His, the Exalted's, will there is an indication (iydhan) that its time is not fixed, but rather it follows His will. It is also read (qurii'a) as: (nasharahu) ("He raised him", with the verb in the form fa'ala without the prefix).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verse 23:

﴿Nay⁠﻿—﴾ a rebuke to man for what he is upon (p-111). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him﴾, is an explanation of the cause of the rebuke, meaning: from Adam, peace be upon him, until this final point, despite the great length of time and its extension, he has not yet fulfilled everything that God Most High commanded him; for no one is free of some shortcoming. Thus they have said, and thus it has been reported from Mujahid and Qatadah. There is no doubt that the thrust of the noble verses is to demonstrate the extreme gravity of man's offence and the realization of his excessive ingratitude, which deserves a great wrath; and it is evident that this is not realized by this degree of shortcoming, which none of its individuals is free from. How could it be otherwise, when the Prayer and Peace of God be upon him said: "Surah Hud has turned me grey, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So be upright as you have been commanded﴾." Therefore the correct reading is that the non-fulfilment should be taken as a negation of comprehensiveness (ʿumum al-nafy) and not as a comprehensive negation (nafy al-ʿumum). This may be either because the one judged is the self-sufficient (al-mustaghni), or because it is the species (al-jins), but not absolutely; rather, the referent of the judgement of non-fulfilment is some of its individuals, yet it is attributed to all of them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, man is greatly unjust and ungrateful﴾, for the sake of intensifying the blame by way of homogeneity (al-mujanasa), in the manner of their saying: "The sons of so-and-so killed so-and-so," when the killer is only one of them. Or it may be that its referent is the whole in respect of being a whole, by way of lifting a universal affirmation (raf al-ijab al-kulli) and not a universal negation (al-salb al-kulli). So the meaning is: not all of its individuals have fulfilled what He commanded him, rather some of them have neglected it through disbelief and disobedience, although what has been detailed of the various kinds of blessings, which encompass all, requires that none of them be exempt from it at all. This is what has been said. It has also been said that ﴿Nay⁠﻿—﴾ means "truly," so it is connected to what follows, meaning: truly he has not acted upon what He commanded him.

Let the human being look at his food. This begins an enumeration of the blessings related to his sustenance after the detailing of the blessings related to his origin; that is: let him look at his food, upon which the affair of his livelihood revolves, how We arranged it. And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verse 25:

﴿Indeed, We poured down the water, pouring[-down].﴾ That is: the rain (al-ghayth). It is a substitutive apposition (badal ishtimal) of "his food," because water is the cause of the food's coming into being, so it encompasses it. It was also read as "innā" (إنّا) as a resumptive new sentence (isti'naf), and it was read as "annā" (أنّى) with imala (the vowel-inclining of the alif, pronounced towards the i-sound), meaning: "How did We pour...?" to its end; that is, We poured it, pouring, in a wondrous manner.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verse 26:

﴿Then We split the earth⦅ ⦆﴾, that is: with plants.

﴿A splitting⦅ ⦆﴾, wondrous and fitting for what splits it of plants in smallness and largeness, shape and form. Taking its splitting to refer to the plowing (al-kirab, i.e. the plowing of the soil) by ascribing it to the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah) as a case of ascribing an act to its cause (isnad al-fi'l ila sababihi) is rejected by the word "thumma" (then) and the "fa'" (so) in His Exalted saying:

So We caused grain to grow therein. The splitting in the aforementioned sense has no sequential connection at all with the rains, nor with the growth of grain without interval. Rather, the sequence is between the rains, the aforementioned splitting, and the growth of grain without interval. The intended meaning of "growth" is what sprouts from the earth until its growth is complete and the grain sets firm. The splitting of the earth by the plant continues to increase and widen until it reaches that stage. Moreover, the course of the noble discourse is to explain the bounties overflowing from His presence, exalted be He, in a wondrous manner outside the customary habits, as the emphasis of the two verbs with their verbal nouns indicates. So interposing the act of the one upon whom the favour is bestowed in the attainment of those bounties disrupts the intended purpose,

(p-112) ﴿And grapes and fodder﴾. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And grapes﴾ is conjoined (ʿatf) to "grain" (ḥabban). It is not a requirement of conjunction that the conjoined element be restricted by all the restrictions that apply to the element it is conjoined to. So there is no harm in grapes growing without the splitting of the earth.

﴿And fodder (qaḍban)﴾, that is, green herbage. It was named by the verbal noun of "qaḍabahu," meaning he cut it, in hyperbole, as if, because of the repetition of its being cut and the multiplicity of cutting, it were the very act of cutting itself.

I need to translate this passage. The Arabic: "﴿وَزَيْتُونًا ونَخْلا﴾ الكَلامُ فِيهِما وفي أمْثالِهِما كَما في العِنَبِ."

Translation:

﴿And olive trees and palm trees﴾. The discussion regarding these two, and regarding their likes, is as it is regarding the grape vine.

And gardens of dense trees (ḥadā'iq ghulban). That is, great ones. The gardens are described with this (word) because of their thickness and the abundance of their trees, or because they have thick trees; it is borrowed from the description of necks (riqāb), (where ghulb means thick-necked).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verse 31:

﴿And fruit and pasture﴾. That is: "abb (pasture), from "abbahu" when one "ammahu," i.e., intended it, because it is sought out and visited; or from "abba li-kadha" when one prepares for something, because it is prepared for grazing; or dry fruit that is gathered for the winter. It is reported from al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) that he was asked about al-abb and said: "What sky would shade me, and what earth would bear me, if I said in the Book of Allah what I have no knowledge of?!" And from 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): that he recited this verse and said: "We have known all of this, so what is al-abb?" Then he threw down a staff that was in his hand and said: "By Allah's life, this is indeed affectation (al-takalluf). And what harm is it to you, O son of Umm 'Umar, that you do not know what al-abb is?" Then he said: "Follow what has been made clear to you from this Book, and leave what is not."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verse 32:

﴿As a provision for you and your cattle.﴾ It is either an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: He did that as a provision (tamti'an) for you and your livestock, for some of the enumerated bounties are food for them and some of them are fodder for their beasts. The shift (al-iltifat) from address to the third person is to complete the reminder of favor (al-imtinan). Or it is an absolute object (masdar mu'akkid) of its implied verb, with the additional elements omitted, meaning: He provided for you with that as a provision (mata'akum bidhalika mata'an). Or it is the absolute object of a verb that follows from it, meaning: He provided for you with that, so you enjoyed a provision (fatamatta'tum mata'an), i.e., an enjoyment (tamatt'an), as has passed more than once. Or it is an absolute object from a verb of the same root in meaning rather than in wording, for what was mentioned of the three verbs carries the meaning of providing (al-tamti').

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verse 33:

﴿Then when the Ṣākhkhah (the deafening blast) comes﴾ This begins the explanation of the states of their return (ma'ād), following the explanation of the origin of their creation and their livelihood. The fa' (then) indicates that what follows is consequent upon what precedes it, namely the various kinds of blessings, which will soon come to an end, as the word matā' (provision, enjoyment) suggests by its implication of the swift cessation of these things and the nearness of their vanishing. And "al-Ṣākhkhah" is the great calamity by which all creatures will be struck deaf, that is, they will incline their ears to it, from (ṣakhkha li-ḥadīthihi), meaning he inclined to his speech and listened to it with pleasure. The second blast (al-nafkhah al-thāniyah) has been described by this name because people will listen attentively to it. It has also been said that it is the cry that deafens the ears, that is, it deafens them because of the severity of its impact. And it has been said that it is derived from ṣakhkahu bi-l-ḥajar, meaning he struck it with the stone.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verse 34:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day a man flees from his brother﴾

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verses 35–36:

﴿And his mother and his father﴾ ﴿and his companion and his sons﴾. ﴿And his mother and his father﴾, ﴿and his companion and his sons﴾ are either in the accusative, governed by "a'ni" (I mean), as an explanation of al-Sakhkha (the Deafening Blast); or they are a substitute (badal) for it, built on fatha because of its being attached to a verb, according to the opinion of the Kufans. It has also been said that it is a substitute for "idha ja'at" (when it comes), as was mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the Day when man remembers﴾ ... etc. That is: he turns away from them and does not keep their company, nor asks about their condition as he did in the world, because he is occupied with his own state. As for explaining this by his knowledge that they will not avail him anything, or by his fear of being held to account for their dues, this is rejected by His saying, exalted is He: *

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verses 35–36:

﴿And his mother and his father﴾ ﴿and his companion and his sons﴾. ﴿And his mother and his father﴾, ﴿and his companion and his sons﴾ are either in the accusative, governed by "a'ni" (I mean), as an explanation of al-Sakhkha (the Deafening Blast); or they are a substitute (badal) for it, built on fatha because of its being attached to a verb, according to the opinion of the Kufans. It has also been said that it is a substitute for "idha ja'at" (when it comes), as was mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the Day when man remembers﴾ ... etc. That is: he turns away from them and does not keep their company, nor asks about their condition as he did in the world, because he is occupied with his own state. As for explaining this by his knowledge that they will not avail him anything, or by his fear of being held to account for their dues, this is rejected by His saying, exalted is He: *

For every man among them that Day, there will be a matter that will occupy him (﴿لِكُلِّ امْرِئٍ مِنهم يَوْمَئِذٍ شَأْنٌ يُغْنِيهِ﴾). This is a resumptive clause (istinaf) that comes to explain the cause of the fleeing. That is, each one of those mentioned has a preoccupation that absorbs him and a grave matter that is enough to keep him concerned with it. As for fleeing out of fear of their demands, or out of hatred for them, as is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: Qabil flees from his brother Habil, the Prophet (ﷺ) flees from his mother, Ibrahim (peace be upon him) flees from his father, Nuh (peace be upon him) flees from his son, and Lut (peace be upon him) flees from his wife. This is not the kind of fleeing meant here. Likewise, what is related, that a man flees from his companions and relatives so that they do not see him in the bad state he is in, is not of this kind either. The word "يَعْنِيهِ" was also read (as a variant recitation, qira'a) with an open yā' and an unpointed ʿayn, meaning "يَهَمَّهُ" (it concerns him), from "عناه الأمر" when the matter caused him worry, that is, when it put him into anxiety. From this is the hadith: "Part of the goodness of a person's Islam is his leaving what does not concern him." It does not come from "عناه" meaning "قصده" (he intended it), as has been said.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verse 38:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾ is an explanation of the final outcome of those previously mentioned and their division into the fortunate (al-su'ada') and the wretched (al-ashqiya'), after the mention of their falling into a calamity that is a great calamity. So "wujuh" (faces) is the subject (mubtada'), even though it is indefinite, because it falls within the scope of classification (fi hayyiz al-tanwi'). "Musfirah" (radiant) is its predicate (khabar), and "yawma'idhin" (that Day) is related to it. That is: shining and beaming, from asfara al-subh (the dawn became bright), meaning when it lit up. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that this refers to the night prayer (qiyam al-layl). And in a hadith: "Whoever prays much at night, his face will be beautiful by day." And it is narrated from al-Dahhak that it refers to the traces of wudu' (ablution). It has also been said: from how much they were covered with dust in the way of Allah.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verse 39:

﴿Laughing, rejoicing﴾ at what they witness of everlasting bliss and lasting delight.

And faces that day will be upon them dust-colored, (Qur'an 80:40)... 

Let me be precise and follow the instructions: translate the passage faithfully.

**Translation:**

﴿And faces, that Day, will have upon them dust﴾, i.e., dust (ghubar) and gloom (kudurah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verse 41:

﴿Covering them﴾ i.e., overtaking them and enveloping them.

﴿Dust﴾ i.e., blackness and darkness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 80, verse 42:

(p-114) ﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the possessors of those faces, and the sense of distance within it is to signal the remoteness of their rank in wretched condition; that is: those described as having blackness upon their faces and what else.

﴿They are the disbelievers, the wicked-doers﴾ who combine disbelief (kufr) and wickedness (fujur). Therefore, God Most High has added to the blackness of their faces the dust (al-ghabarah).

From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah 'Abasa, he will come on the Day of Resurrection with a face that is laughing and joyful."
